meeting.who: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand (“the RBNZ”, often called “the Reserve Bank”), New Zealand’s central bank. Its interest rate decisions are made by the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC), chaired by Governor Anna Breman. The MPC tries to agree as a group (by “consensus”). When it cannot, it votes, and since May 2026 each member’s vote is published by name. From October 15 the Committee gains a seventh member, Rebecca Williams.

what_changed.headline: Q3 2026 inflation came in at 3.7%, falling from Q2's 4.1% but remaining above the 1%–3% target band.
items: Consumers price index (CPI) fell from 4.1% in Q2 2026 to 3.7% in Q3 2026 (Stats NZ).
Non-tradables inflation eased slightly from 3.4% in Q2 2026 to 3.3% in Q3 2026.
Tradables inflation dropped from 4.9% in Q2 2026 to 4.3% in Q3 2026.
Brent crude oil declined from $126.55 on October 14 to $115.22 a barrel on October 20.
Because inflation came in cooler than the RBNZ's 3.9% forecast, our verdict shifts from a 55% chance of a Raise to a 55% chance of a Hold.

verdict.headline: HOLD
verdict.sub: Keep the interest rate where it is, at 2.75%. Inflation has cooled to 3.7%, easing pressure for an immediate rate rise ahead of the October 28 decision.
verdict.confidence_note: “Low” means this remains a close call. While Q3 CPI cooled to 3.7%, oil remains elevated and the October 28 meeting is a shorter Review without full new forecasts.
verdict.short_version: New Zealand annual inflation cooled to 3.7% in the September quarter, down from 4.1% in June but still above the 1%–3% target band. With GDP growth sluggish at 0.2% and unemployment at 5.6%, the cooler-than-expected inflation print gives the RBNZ room to pause on October 28 rather than press the brake for a third consecutive meeting.
verdict.card_why: Q3 inflation cooled to 3.7% (below the 3.9% forecast), supporting a pause despite lingering oil pressures.
verdict.last_move: Raised 0.25 pts on Sep 2, 2026 (second rise in a row)

why_steps.title: The RBNZ has one main job, and one main tool
why_steps.html: The Reserve Bank’s main job is to keep prices steady. Its target is that prices should rise between 1% and 3% a year, aiming for the 2% midpoint over the medium term. It also tries to avoid unnecessary swings in jobs and output, so it watches unemployment closely. Its main tool is the Official Cash Rate, or OCR. In the RBNZ’s words, it is “the interest rate that banks earn on their deposits with us”, and it also sets what banks pay when they borrow from the Reserve Bank. That flows through to floating mortgages, business loans and savings accounts. Think of it like the pedals of a car. Raising the OCR is pressing the brake: loans get more expensive, so people and companies borrow and spend less, and prices cool down. Cutting is pressing the gas. Holding means keeping your foot where it is. Today the OCR is 2.75%. In July the RBNZ described the rate as still “accommodative”, meaning it is still giving the economy a little gas (July record).

why_steps.title: Prices are above the band, but Q3 CPI came in cooler than expected
why_steps.html: Consumer prices (the CPI, or consumers price index, from Stats NZ) were 3.7% higher in the September 2026 quarter than a year earlier, cooling from 4.1% in the June quarter (Stats NZ). In simple terms: a basket of everyday things that cost NZ$100 a year ago now costs about NZ$103.70. The goal would be about NZ$102. Unlike most countries, New Zealand measures the CPI only once every three months, so each report is a big event. Look underneath. In August, petrol was up 17.9% and diesel 45.8% on a year earlier (Treasury). The worry remains the home-grown part: prices of things that cannot be imported, like rent, insurance and services (“non-tradables”), are rising 3.3%, down slightly from 3.4% (RBNZ September MPS). The RBNZ had forecast annual inflation of 3.9% for the September quarter, so the actual 3.7% outcome provides welcome relief.

why_steps.title: So the RBNZ has pressed the brake twice
why_steps.html: After cutting the OCR to 2.25% in late 2025, the RBNZ held through May. In May the Committee split 3–3, and Governor Breman’s casting vote kept the rate on hold (RBNZ). It then raised to 2.50% on July 8 and to 2.75% on September 2, both times by consensus. In September it said: “Conditional on the central economic outlook, members judged that the OCR may need to increase further.” Its own projection has the OCR rising to about 3.2% over the next two years, which implies roughly two more 0.25-point rises (RBNZ). The mood inside the Committee has also shifted. In July, two of six members saw the risks to inflation as tilted upward. By September it was four of six (Gourley, Silk, Gai and Governor Breman), with Conway and Hansen seeing risks as balanced.

why_steps.title: Reasons the RBNZ might hold in October
why_steps.html:
• Inflation cooled more than expected. Q3 CPI came in at 3.7%, below the RBNZ's 3.9% forecast.
  • The economy is weak. GDP grew only 0.2% in the June quarter and household spending was flat (Stats NZ). Unemployment is 5.6%, and the RBNZ expects it to stay above 5% until 2028.
  • Bond markets already pressed the brake. The 10-year government bond rate is 5.00%. Fixed mortgage rates follow these wholesale rates.
  • December brings full forecasts. October is a shorter Review without full new forecasts.
  • “May”, not “will”. September’s wording (“may need to increase further”) was softer than July’s (“further OCR increases appear likely”).

why_steps.title: Reasons the RBNZ might still raise in October
why_steps.html:
• Oil is far above what the RBNZ assumed. Its September forecasts assumed Dubai oil of about US$85 a barrel for the September quarter. Brent oil was $115.22 a barrel on October 20. Governor Breman noted that persistent high oil prices risk near-term inflation (RBNZ).
  • The Kiwi dollar is weaker than assumed. The RBNZ assumed a trade-weighted index of 66.9, but it stood at 63.94 on October 14. A weaker currency makes imported fuel and goods dearer.
  • The Committee’s balance has tilted. Four of six members saw upside inflation risk in September.
  • Other central banks are braking. The U.S. Fed rate top is 4.00% and the ECB’s deposit rate is 2.50%.

why_steps.title: Weighing both sides

left: Inflation at 3.7% is still above the 1%–3% band
Oil remains well above the RBNZ’s assumption
Weaker Kiwi dollar pushes up import costs
4 of 6 members saw upside inflation risk in September
right: Bond rates near 5% doing tightening work
October is a shorter Review; December has full forecasts

why_steps.html: Both sides are close. What tips us slightly toward Hold is that the September quarter inflation print came in at 3.7%, below the RBNZ's 3.9% expectation. Combined with fragile growth and 5.6% unemployment, the central bank has breathing room to keep the OCR at 2.75% while assessing data. That is why we say about 55% Hold, 42% Raise and 3% Cut.

why_steps.title: The one thing to watch: employment indicators
why_steps.html: With the October 28 decision and employment indicators report arriving on the same day, the focus shifts to whether job market slack and wage growth continue to keep domestic price pressures contained.

timeline.title: The RBNZ cut the OCR three times, to 2.25%
timeline.what: The OCR went from 3.25% to 3.00% in August, to 2.50% in October (a big 0.50-point cut) and to 2.25% in November. The November cut was decided by a 5–1 vote; the RBNZ did not name the dissenter.
timeline.why: The economy had shrunk in the June 2025 quarter by more than expected, and there was lots of spare capacity. In October the Committee weighed 0.25 against 0.50 and chose the bigger cut. Inflation was around the top of the band (3.0% in the September 2025 quarter), but expected to fall back to 2%.
timeline.people: Floating mortgage rates and business loans got cheaper. Term deposits paid less.
timeline.because: with the OCR well below “neutral”, the RBNZ stopped to let the cuts work.

timeline.title: A new Governor, a pause at 2.25%
timeline.what: At her first Monetary Policy Statement as chair, Governor Anna Breman’s Committee held the OCR. It noted “Annual consumers price inflation increased to 3.1 percent in the December 2025 quarter” and “the unemployment rate increased to 5.4 percent”. It said: “If the economy evolves as expected, monetary policy is likely to remain accommodative for some time.”
timeline.why: Growth had bounced back (GDP +1.1% in the September 2025 quarter), and inflation was expected to fall toward 2% within a year. There was no reason to press either pedal.
timeline.people: Borrowing costs stayed low. Most talk was about when, much later, rates might start to rise.
timeline.because: the RBNZ was sitting still with its foot near the gas when a new shock arrived from the Middle East.

timeline.title: The Middle East conflict: an oil shock
timeline.what: Conflict in the Middle East “significantly reduced the supply of oil, gas and other petrochemicals” through the Strait of Hormuz. On April 8 the RBNZ held at 2.25% (by consensus), forecast inflation of 4.2% for the June quarter, and warned that if fuel started pushing up other prices, “decisive and timely increases in the OCR would be required.”
timeline.why: New Zealand imports all of its fuel. Dearer oil means dearer petrol, diesel, freight and flights, which feed into many prices. But it also squeezes household budgets, which slows the economy.
timeline.people: Filling the car got much more expensive within weeks. The RBNZ noted households were already facing “weak real income growth, high unemployment and house price weakness.”
timeline.because: the question became: will the RBNZ “look through” the fuel jump, or brake to stop it spreading?

timeline.title: A 3–3 split, settled by the Governor
timeline.what: The Committee split evenly. Breman, Silk and Conway voted to hold at 2.25%; Hansen, Gourley and Gai voted to raise to 2.50%. The Governor’s casting vote kept the rate on hold. The RBNZ said “the OCR will most likely need to increase sooner and by more than envisaged” and that it expected rises “this year”. March quarter inflation was 3.1%.
timeline.why: Half the Committee wanted to act early against inflation; the other half worried more about weak growth (2026 growth was cut by 0.9 points).
timeline.people: For the first time, New Zealanders could see each member’s vote, thanks to new transparency rules from April 30. Markets started preparing for rises.
timeline.because: a rise at the next meeting looked very likely.

timeline.title: First rise: the OCR goes to 2.50%
timeline.what: The RBNZ raised by 0.25 points, by consensus. Oil had dropped after “the partial reopening of the Strait of Hormuz”, but the RBNZ said the effects “will linger for some time”. It added: “while further OCR increases appear likely at upcoming meetings, their timing is highly uncertain.”
timeline.why: Inflation was expected to peak at 3.9% in the June quarter and stay above the band for several quarters. The Committee judged the OCR was still “accommodative”, giving the economy gas it no longer needed.
timeline.people: Floating mortgage rates rose a little. Savers started to earn slightly more.
timeline.because: everyone waited for the June quarter price and job numbers.

timeline.title: Inflation 4.1%, unemployment 5.6%
timeline.what: CPI inflation came in at 4.1%, above the RBNZ’s July estimate of 3.9%. Without fuel it was 2.9%. Unemployment rose to 5.6%. Wage rates rose only 2.0% a year.
timeline.people: A household whose costs were NZ$1,000 a week a year ago now paid about NZ$1,041, while pay rose only about NZ$20 per NZ$1,000.
timeline.because: the RBNZ judged that inflation was the bigger danger.

timeline.title: Second rise: the OCR goes to 2.75%
timeline.what: In its September Monetary Policy Statement the RBNZ raised by 0.25 points, by consensus: “Inflation increased to 4.1 percent in the June quarter because of higher fuel prices arising from the conflict in the Middle East.” It said the OCR “may need to increase further”, forecast 3.9% inflation for the September quarter, and projected the OCR rising to about 3.2%.
timeline.people: Mortgage rates for 6-month to 2-year terms had already risen 0.20–0.30 points since May, and the Kiwi dollar rose a little as investors expected more rises.
timeline.because: markets began pricing another rise for October.

timeline.title: A weak economy, and markets expect more
timeline.what: GDP grew only 0.2% in the June quarter, with household spending flat. Treasury said markets priced about a 70% chance of an October rise. On September 29 Treasury’s pre-election update said “An emerging economic recovery has been delayed by higher oil prices.”
timeline.people: House prices were 0.9% lower than a year earlier in August, and house sales were down 13%. Many people felt poorer.
timeline.because: the October call hinged on whether new shocks pushed inflation risk up further. They did.

timeline.title: Oil spikes, the Kiwi dollar slides
timeline.what: Brent oil rose toward $126.55 by mid-October before easing back to $115.22. One NZ dollar fell to US$0.5621, and the New Zealand 10-year bond rate reached 5.00%. Governor Breman noted the challenging global environment.
timeline.people: Fuel prices at the pump stayed high, and imported goods remained dearer.
timeline.because: the case for a pause strengthened as inflation data arrived.

timeline.title: Q3 CPI comes in at 3.7%
timeline.what: Stats NZ reported Q3 2026 annual CPI inflation at 3.7%, below the RBNZ's 3.9% forecast. The OCR is 2.75%, the 2-year government bond yield 3.94%, the 10-year 5.00%, and the trade-weighted index 63.94. The October Review takes place on October 28.
timeline.because: cooler inflation of 3.7% makes a Hold our primary expectation for October 28.

choices.title: Hold: keep the OCR at 2.75%
choices.meaning: the RBNZ keeps its foot where it is for now, reacting to cooler Q3 inflation (3.7%) while acknowledging that further rises remain possible down the track.
for: Inflation is cooling. Q3 CPI fell to 3.7%, below the RBNZ's 3.9% forecast.
Weak growth and high unemployment. GDP grew only 0.2% and unemployment is 5.6%.
Bond markets did some of the work. The 10-year rate is 5.00%.
December is a better moment for full new forecasts and labour market updates.
Softer wording. September’s “may need to increase further” leaves room to pause.
against: Oil and the currency remain challenging. Brent is at $115.22 and the trade-weighted index is 63.94.
Inflation is still above target. 3.7% is above the 1%–3% band.
choices.everyday: floating loan and savings rates would stay about where they are for now.

choices.title: Raise: up 0.25 points, to 3.00%
choices.meaning: the RBNZ presses the brake for the third meeting in a row to ensure inflation returns decisively to the 2% midpoint.
for: Inflation remains above target. At 3.7%, headline inflation is still above the 1%–3% band.
Oil and currency pressures. Brent oil ($115.22) and a weaker Kiwi dollar (63.94 TWI) continue to push up import costs.
The Committee leans hawkish. Four of six members saw upside inflation risk in September.
against: Q3 inflation came in lower than expected (3.7% vs 3.9%), removing some urgency for an immediate hike.
Fragile economic activity. GDP growth is weak and unemployment is 5.6%.
choices.everyday: floating mortgage rates would rise by roughly a quarter point.

choices.title: Cut: lower the OCR
choices.meaning: the RBNZ would switch from the brake to the gas.
for: Only in an emergency: for example a sudden financial crisis or severe economic collapse.
against: Inflation is 3.7%. Cutting would add fuel to above-target price pressures.
The RBNZ’s own track points up, to about 3.2%.
choices.everyday: loans would get slightly cheaper, but it would signal severe economic distress.

change.lead: Our 55% / 42% / 3% forecast reflects the cooler Q3 inflation print (3.7%) published on October 22. Here is what we are watching next.
change.intro: The RBNZ can only react to information it has already seen. A report released before October 28 can change the October decision. A report released after it can only shape December 9.

consumers_price_index_cpi.trigger: Prompted our shift from Raise to Hold.

change.other_title: Other things that could move our view
other: Oil and the Middle East. Brent is at $115.22 a barrel. A sustained move back below US$100 would make waiting much easier.
The Kiwi dollar. A further slide below US$0.55 would add to imported inflation.
Final words from the RBNZ. Any speech or interview before October 28 is a direct hint.
Bond markets. If the 10-year rate (5.00%) falls back sharply, one argument for Hold strengthens.

report_card.one: Prices are 3.7% higher than a year ago, still above the 1%–3% band.
report_card.look: Consumer prices (CPI, up 3.7%), non-tradables (3.3%), and inflation expectations.
report_card.why: Headline inflation cooled from 4.1% to 3.7% in Q3, beating the RBNZ's 3.9% forecast. However, it remains above the target band, and oil and currency pressures persist.
report_card.change: Inflation returning inside the 1%–3% target band.
report_card.matters: Prices remain the primary reason the RBNZ tightened policy, though the cooler Q3 print provides breathing room.

report_card.one: Unemployment is high at 5.6%, but hiring is slowly picking up.
report_card.look: The quarterly unemployment rate, monthly filled jobs, job ads, and wage growth.
report_card.why: Unemployment rose to 5.6%, but monthly filled jobs and job ads show modest recovery. Not bad enough to be red, not healthy enough to be green.
report_card.change: Unemployment rising toward 6% → red. Unemployment falling → green.
report_card.matters: This is a key reason the RBNZ may pause rate hikes.

report_card.one: Exporters are doing well, but households are holding back.
report_card.look: GDP, household spending, retail sales, exports, business confidence and house prices.
report_card.why: GDP rose only 0.2% in Q2 and household spending was flat. Retail volumes fell 0.5%. Conversely, goods exports were up 12.3% in September from a year earlier.
report_card.change: Clear signs of a household spending pick-up → green.
report_card.matters: A weak economy makes each rate rise more painful.

report_card.one: Borrowing costs have jumped, and the Kiwi dollar is weak.
report_card.look: Wholesale interest rates and the NZ dollar.
report_card.why: The 10-year government bond rate is 5.00%. The NZ dollar sits at US$0.5621, and the trade-weighted index is 63.94.
report_card.change: A calmer currency and lower long rates → green.
report_card.matters: Higher market rates cool borrowing, supporting a pause.

said.v: New framework supports access to basic services
w: What it said: “The Reserve Bank of New Zealand – Te Pūtea Matua (RBNZ) has brought together public and private sector organisations to sign a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) aimed at supporting access to basic transaction services in New Zealand.”
Why it matters: shows ongoing coordination to ensure public access to core financial services.

What it said: “The Australian Prudential Regulation Authority (APRA) and the Reserve Bank of New Zealand – Te Pūtea Matua (RBNZ) have completed the 2026 Trans-Tasman Stress Test, their first joint stress testing exercise since 2017.”
Why it matters: highlights ongoing cross-border banking cooperation and financial stability checks.

said.v: RBNZ and FMA outline AI risks
w: What it said: “The Reserve Bank of New Zealand – Te Pūtea Matua (RBNZ) and the Financial Markets Authority – Te Mana Tātai Hokohoko (FMA) have today outlined their supervisory expectations on cyber risks associated with frontier Artificial Intelligence (AI).”
Why it matters: shows regulators actively guiding financial institutions on emerging technology risks.
What it said: A new internal member of the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC), Rebecca Williams, has been appointed by the Minister of Finance, Nicola Willis, on the recommendation of the RBNZ Board.
Why it matters: brings a fresh internal economic voice to the October decision table.
What it said: “Conditional on the central economic outlook, members judged that the OCR may need to increase further.” The decision was by consensus.
Why it matters: the RBNZ is openly signalling more rises, but uses the softer word “may”.

What it said: Gourley, Silk, Gai and Breman saw inflation risks to the upside; Conway and Hansen saw them as balanced, with downside risks to activity. All agreed downside activity risks were significant.
Why it matters: in July only two members (Gai, Gourley) saw upside risk. The Committee has moved toward worrying more about inflation.

said.v: Oil and long rates a challenge
w: What it said: “If higher oil prices persist, they are expected to result in somewhat higher near-term inflation” and “As always, we will assess incoming data and global developments ahead of our next decision in October”.
Why it matters: it is the latest on-the-record comment we found. It flags oil as the key risk but does not pre-commit.
What it said: “businesses pass on cost increases more readily now than in the past” and “anchored inflation expectations cannot be taken for granted”.
Why it matters: it explains why the RBNZ does not simply ignore a fuel shock, even though Conway was one of the members seeing balanced risks in September.

gaps: Up-to-date market odds for October. The only figure we found is Treasury’s mid-September reading of about 70%, before the latest oil spike and Q3 CPI print. Why it matters: we cannot precisely compare our 55% chance of a hold with what markets expect today.

Full Stats NZ releases. For the Q3 CPI and other releases we could read only headline summaries; further details come from RBNZ and Treasury summaries. Why it matters: small details could differ from full official tables.
Individual core inflation measures and household inflation expectations were not collected; we have only the RBNZ’s average and description.
Recent speeches. We found no MPC speech between Governor Breman’s September 22 Dunedin remarks and today.
Who votes in October. We assume seven members, but the RBNZ has not confirmed attendance.
How we gathered data: data were gathered via web search and direct page reads on October 22, 2026.

group_intros.prices: These numbers tell us how fast things are getting more expensive in New Zealand. The RBNZ’s job is to keep yearly inflation between 1% and 3%, aiming for the 2% midpoint over the medium term. New Zealand measures consumer prices quarterly.
group_intros.jobs: These numbers show whether New Zealanders can find work and how fast pay is rising. Spare workers help keep wage and price growth in check.
group_intros.growth: These numbers show how fast New Zealand’s economy is growing and whether households are spending. Weak growth argues for a gentler brake.
group_intros.rates: The OCR is the RBNZ’s main lever. Market interest rates show what investors expect the RBNZ to do next.
group_intros.said: What the Reserve Bank and its Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) have said, in their own words. Quotes are verbatim from the linked pages.
group_intros.global: New Zealand imports all its crude oil and fuel and sells much of what it makes overseas, so world energy prices and other central banks matter a lot.

copy.story_intro: This is the story of the past year, in order. Each step explains what happened, why it happened, and what it meant for ordinary people. The line at the bottom of each step (“Because of this…”) shows how it led to the next step, so you can follow cause and effect from start to finish.
copy.choices_intro: At every meeting the RBNZ has three options. Below we explain what each one would mean, why it could happen, why it might not, and what it would mean in everyday life. Analysis · our judgement
copy.report_intro: Think of this as a school report for the economy in four subjects. Green means healthy. Yellow means mixed, keep watching. Red means a problem the central bank must fix. Each grade is also written in words, so you do not need to see the color. Analysis
copy.gaps_intro: Good research is honest about its blind spots. Here is what is missing, delayed or unverified, and why it matters.
copy.numbers_intro: Every number we used, grouped by topic. For each one you will see the latest value, the period it covers, when it was published, the previous value, where it came from, and, most importantly, a plain explanation of what it is and why it matters. Tap a group to open or close it. Observed facts

live_before.html: The numbers on this page are a snapshot taken on October 14, 2026. If you want to see whether anything has changed since then, you can try loading the newest values from FRED, a free public data service run by the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis. Note: FRED does not carry an up-to-date New Zealand CPI series (its OECD copy stops in early 2025), so for prices use Stats NZ and the RBNZ directly. Several New Zealand series on FRED are monthly or quarterly OECD copies that arrive months late, and its unemployment copy (5.3% for the March quarter) differs slightly from Stats NZ’s published 5.4%. For daily interest and exchange rates, the RBNZ’s own statistics pages are more current.

How it works: FRED gives anyone a free “API key”, a code that works like a library card for its data. Paste your key below and press Refresh. The newest values appear in a separate table, next to our snapshot values so you can compare. The rest of this page stays exactly as it is.
Privacy: your key is saved only in this browser, on this device, and is sent only to FRED. Press “Forget key” to remove it. Get a free key at fred.stlouisfed.org.

live_after.html: Good to know: FRED often does not allow web pages to request its data directly, so many browsers will block this. If that happens, you will see a clear message and nothing on the page will change. You can always check the same numbers yourself on the FRED website.

summary.headline: Q3 2026 inflation came in at 3.7%, falling from Q2's 4.1% but remaining above the 1%–3% target band.
items: Consumers price index (CPI) fell from 4.1% in Q2 2026 to 3.7% in Q3 2026 (Stats NZ).
Non-tradables inflation eased slightly from 3.4% in Q2 2026 to 3.3% in Q3 2026.
Tradables inflation dropped from 4.9% in Q2 2026 to 4.3% in Q3 2026.
Brent crude oil declined from $126.55 on October 14 to $115.22 a barrel on October 20.
Because inflation came in cooler than the RBNZ's 3.9% forecast, our verdict shifts from a 55% chance of a Raise to a 55% chance of a Hold.

summary.headline: 10-year government bond yields rose slightly to 5.07%, while other economic data remained steady ahead of the October 28 meeting.
items: 10-year government bond yields increased from 5.02% on October 19 to 5.07% on October 20 (Trading Economics).
No official interest rate decision or monetary policy statement has been released since September 2; our verdict and probabilities remain unchanged.

summary.headline: Goods exports rose 12.3% in September from a year earlier, while other economic data remained steady.
items: Goods exports increased by +12.3% vs a year ago in September, compared to +15.4% in August (Stats NZ).
No official interest rate decision or monetary policy statement has been released since September 2; our verdict and probabilities remain unchanged.
